title: Entities, Not Distributed Transactions: Pat Helland's Case for Local-Only Consistency
objective: Reason about why distributed transactions across partitioned data don't scale in practice, and model data as independent entities -- locally transactional, coordinated across boundaries through messaging rather than a shared transaction.

content_blocks.heading: The Promise Distributed Transactions Rarely Keep
content_blocks.body:
A distributed transaction promises the same all-or-nothing guarantee a single-machine transaction gives, just coordinated across several machines through protocols like two-phase commit. Pat Helland's 2007 paper "Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion" argues this promise rarely holds up at real scale: large systems consistently avoid relying on it in practice, not because the protocols are theoretically wrong, but because the coordination cost and fragility make it impractical once enough machines and enough scale are actually involved.

This session covers his proposed alternative directly: modeling data as independent "entities," each one a bounded unit that stays transactional on its own, with cross-boundary work handled through messaging instead of a shared transaction spanning multiple entities at once.

The paper is a position paper from CIDR 2007, not a specific product recommendation -- the underlying argument has only gotten more relevant as systems have grown more distributed since then.

reference_links.label: Pat Helland -- Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate's Opinion

content_blocks.heading: Why Coordination Across Machines Gets Fragile Fast
content_blocks.body:
A two-phase-commit-style transaction requires every participating machine to stay available and responsive for the entire duration of the transaction, holding locks the whole time while waiting for every other participant to also agree to commit. One slow or temporarily unreachable participant blocks every other participant -- nobody can finish until the slowest or least available one responds, and the probability that *some* participant is briefly slow or unreachable grows with both the number of participants and how long the transaction holds its locks.

This is a structural property, not a quality-of-implementation problem: even a theoretically correct two-phase-commit implementation is only as reliable as its least reliable participant, for as long as the slowest transaction in flight takes to resolve.

Adding more participants doesn't average out this risk -- it compounds it, since every additional machine is one more opportunity for the whole transaction to stall.

exercises.prompt: A distributed transaction spans five machines using two-phase commit. One of the five becomes briefly unreachable due to a network blip. What happens to the transaction?

options: It stalls -- every other participant has to wait, holding its own locks, until the unreachable machine responds or times out
The other four machines automatically commit on their own, with the unreachable one rejoining the already-finished transaction later
The transaction's outcome depends entirely on which specific machine became unreachable, with no general rule applying here
This has no effect at all, since two-phase commit is specifically designed to tolerate any number of unreachable participants
definition.explanation: Two-phase commit requires every participant's agreement before anyone can finalize -- the other four machines are still holding their own locks, waiting, and can't proceed without hearing from the fifth. This is exactly the fragility Helland's paper describes: reliability is bounded by the least available participant, not an incidental implementation detail that a better protocol version could simply route around.

content_blocks.heading: Entities: Transactions That Never Leave One Machine's Boundary
content_blocks.body:
Helland's alternative models data as belonging to exactly one "entity" at a time -- a bounded, independently-owned unit of data, small enough to live on one machine (or one tightly-coupled replicated group) rather than spread across many. A transaction that stays entirely within one entity's boundary only ever needs that one entity's own cooperation, never a second machine's -- cheap, fast, and reliable in exactly the way a cross-machine transaction structurally can't be.

A bank account is a natural entity: every operation that only touches *one* account's own balance and history -- a deposit, a withdrawal, checking a balance -- can be a fully local, strongly consistent transaction, with nothing outside that one account ever needing to be involved at all.

The entity doesn't have to be a single machine literally -- it can be a small, tightly-coupled replicated group -- as long as every operation on it stays within that one group's own coordination, never reaching out to a second, independent group.

exercises.prompt: A bank models each customer's account as its own entity. A customer deposits money into their own account. Why does this operation avoid the fragility of a distributed transaction?

options: The operation stays entirely within one account's own entity boundary -- it never needs a second machine's cooperation at all
Deposits are inherently simpler operations than withdrawals, which is the actual reason this specific case avoids any fragility
This operation still requires full two-phase commit coordination, but happens to complete quickly enough that nobody notices
Bank account balances are specifically exempt from the coordination requirements that apply to every other kind of data
definition.explanation: A deposit to one account only ever touches that one account's own data -- there's no second entity involved, so there's no second machine to coordinate with and nothing to wait on beyond the one entity already handling the request. This is exactly the shape Helland's model is built around: keep the common case local by drawing entity boundaries around what usually needs to change together.

content_blocks.heading: Crossing Entity Boundaries: Messaging, Not a Shared Transaction
content_blocks.body:
A transfer between two different accounts touches two separate entities -- exactly the case a single shared transaction would otherwise need to span. Helland's model handles this instead as a sequence of local transactions connected by messages: debit the first account (one local, fully consistent transaction), send a message, credit the second account (a second local, fully consistent transaction) -- each step locally atomic, with the overall transfer reaching consistency across both accounts eventually, not instantaneously.

This is the same consistency tradeoff module 35 already covered from the CAP/PACELC angle, now applied concretely to a real operation: within an entity, strong consistency is cheap; across entities, the honest answer is eventual consistency achieved through a sequence of messages, not a single atomic instant spanning both.

The gap between the debit and the credit is real and has to be designed for explicitly -- a crash between the two steps leaves the system in an intermediate state that recovery logic has to know how to resolve.

exercises.prompt: A transfer debits account A and credits account B, implemented as two separate local transactions connected by a message, rather than one transaction spanning both accounts. What consistency property does this transfer actually have?

options: Each step is strongly consistent alone; the transfer overall reaches consistency eventually
The entire transfer is strongly consistent at every single instant, exactly matching a true cross-account transaction
Neither step carries any consistency guarantee at all, since splitting the transfer this way removes any guarantee entirely
This design is only valid for small transfers; any larger transfer would require genuine cross-account atomicity instead
definition.explanation: Each local transaction is fully consistent the moment it commits -- account A's debit is real and final, and so is account B's credit. What's eventual is the window between the two steps, during which the money has left A but hasn't yet arrived at B. That's a real, named tradeoff (eventual consistency across the boundary), not an absence of any guarantee at all.

content_blocks.heading: The Real Design Question: Where to Draw Entity Boundaries
content_blocks.body:
This reframes the actual design problem: not "how do we make cross-machine transactions more reliable," but "how do we draw entity boundaries so the common case never needs to cross one." A transfer between two accounts at the *same* bank can often be modeled so both accounts live in one entity if the bank's own data model allows it, keeping that specific transfer fully local. A transfer between two accounts at *different* banks is inherently cross-entity no matter how cleverly boundaries are drawn -- two separate institutions' data will never share one entity.

Good entity design means putting data that usually changes together inside the same boundary, and treating genuinely separate ownership (different banks, different services, different teams' data) as an accepted cross-entity case to handle through messaging, not a problem to eliminate by forcing a shared transaction across a boundary that reflects something real.

exercises.prompt: A system design question is posed as "how do we make our cross-service transactions more reliable," where the two services are owned by entirely separate teams with separate databases. What does Helland's framing suggest about this question itself?

options: May be the wrong question -- better to accept eventual consistency across a genuinely separate ownership boundary
Correctly framed as-is; the only real task left is picking a more robust distributed-transaction protocol to implement it
Impossible to design for at all -- separately-owned data can never be coordinated reliably under any approach whatsoever
The two teams should merge into one shared database first, which would make the original question unnecessary to even ask
definition.explanation: Separately-owned data across separate teams is exactly the case where a shared, strongly-consistent transaction fights against how the data is genuinely organized. Helland's framing suggests redirecting the actual design effort toward accepting and managing eventual consistency across that real boundary -- local transactions plus messaging -- rather than chasing a more reliable version of a coordination pattern that's fighting the data's real ownership structure.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
Distributed transactions promise the same guarantee a local transaction gives, but the coordination cost -- every participant held captive until the slowest one responds -- makes that promise fragile at real scale, which is why large systems consistently avoid relying on it. Modeling data as independent entities keeps the common case local and cheap, and treats a genuine cross-boundary operation as a sequence of local transactions and messages, reaching consistency eventually rather than instantly across the boundary.

The real design skill this session points toward is drawing entity boundaries around what actually needs to change together, so the common case never has to cross one, and accepting the cross-entity case deliberately rather than fighting it with heavier coordination.

The next sessions in this module build on exactly that: ACID and BASE as formal consistency models, and the partitioning and sharding strategies that put entity boundaries into practice at real scale.
